subject: Anatomy
summary: The brainstem links the brain to the spinal cord and houses cranial nerve nuclei and vital autonomic centers. Its anatomy determines clinical signs of focal lesions and guides emergency assessment. Understanding its structure helps localise deficits and predict complications.

sections.p: The brainstem is the central conduit between the cerebrum and spinal cord, containing nuclei for cranial nerves I–XII, reticular formation, and vital autonomic centers. It integrates sensory, motor, and autonomic pathways and is essential for consciousness and life‑sustaining functions.
b: Central to consciousness, breathing, heart rate, and reflexes

sections.p: It extends from the foramen magnum to the pontomedullary sulcus, comprising the midbrain, pons, and medulla. Each segment has characteristic nuclei and tracts: midbrain (oculomotor, red nucleus), pons (trigeminal, abducens, facial), medulla (vagus, glossopharyngeal, hypoglossal).

Anteriorly, the cerebellum and fourth ventricle; posteriorly, the cerebellar peduncles; laterally, the cranial nerves exit. The brainstem lies beneath the tentorium and above the spinal cord, with the medulla forming the lower border of the fourth ventricle.
b: Cranial nerve nuclei lie within the brainstem; exit points are at the surface

sections.p: Three major arterial systems supply the brainstem: the basilar artery (midbrain, pons), the vertebral arteries (medulla), and penetrating branches (e.g., pontine arteries). Adequate perfusion is critical; hypoperfusion leads to infarction.

t.b: Detects large vessel occlusion; a negative result suggests small vessel disease or hemorrhage
Identifies acute infarcts; positive signal indicates cytotoxic edema and irreversible injury

sections.p: Cranial nerve nuclei reside in the brainstem: CN I in the midbrain, II in the midbrain, III–IV in the midbrain, V–XII in the pons and medulla. The reticular formation provides ascending arousal pathways.
b: CN III, IV, V, VI in midbrain
CN VII, IX, X, XI, XII in pons/medulla

sections.p: The brainstem controls basic life functions—respiration, cardiovascular regulation, and arousal. It also coordinates eye movements, facial expression, swallowing, and reflexes such as gag and cough.
b: Regulates breathing via medullary respiratory centers
Maintains heart rate through vagal nuclei

sections.p: Lesions produce characteristic cranial nerve deficits, hemiparesis, and autonomic instability. Duret hemorrhages, often seen in brainstem death, result from transtentorial herniation. In low‑resource settings, infections like TB meningitis or HIV encephalitis can involve the brainstem.
b: Brainstem death: absent reflexes, absent vestibulo‑ocular responses

t.b: Confirm absence of brainstem reflexes and spontaneous respiration; a negative caloric test supports death diagnosis
Detects meningitic or infectious involvement of the brainstem; abnormal CSF indicates inflammation

sections.p: Cranial nerve deficits on the opposite side of a hemiparesis localise the lesion to the contralateral nucleus. Absence of vestibulo‑ocular responses is a key criterion for brainstem death. Duret hemorrhages appear as flame‑shaped lesions on imaging.
b: Opposite‑side cranial nerve deficit = nucleus lesion

sections.p: Treat underlying cause (e.g., antibiotics for TB meningitis, antiretroviral therapy for HIV). Supportive care includes airway protection, ventilation, and hemodynamic monitoring. Avoid drugs that depress respiration or lower intracranial pressure excessively.
Brainstem lesions can mimic cerebellar or cortical strokes; distinguishing cranial nerve nuclei involvement helps differentiate.
b: Cerebellar stroke: ataxia without cranial nerve deficits

sections.p: Normal CT may miss small pontine infarcts; early MRI is more sensitive. CSF opening pressure can be normal in early meningitis, delaying diagnosis.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness with absent brainstem reflexes

faq.q: What is the most common brainstem stroke location?
faq.a: The pons is most frequently affected due to its rich vascular supply and vulnerability to small vessel disease.
By demonstrating absent brainstem reflexes, no spontaneous respiration, and negative vestibulo‑ocular responses on caloric testing.
Yes; TB meningitis, HIV encephalitis, and viral encephalitis can involve the brainstem, leading to cranial nerve deficits and autonomic instability.

exam: Explain how a lesion in the midbrain would produce a contralateral hemiparesis and ipsilateral oculomotor palsy.
Describe the clinical steps to confirm brainstem death in a comatose patient.
Identify the vascular territories supplying the pons and medulla and explain how infarction in each would present clinically.
